summary: The Host Identity Protocol CERT parameter carries digital certificates in HIP control packets. This experimental document defines it and the error signaling for failed verification. It also describes how to represent Host Identity Tags in X.509 v3 and SPKI. It was replaced by RFC 8002.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers using HIP prove who they are with ID cards. This says where in the messages to put the card and how to complain if it is bad. It was later replaced by RFC 8002.

questions: how are certificates carried in hip
what is a host identity tag
subtitle: Carrying and representing certificates in the Host Identity Protocol

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) needs a way to transmit digital certificates in control packets, and needs standard ways to represent host identities (HITs) within those certificates.
tldr.mechanism: The CERT parameter acts as a container for different certificate types (X.509 v3, SPKI, and others), with fields for grouping related certificates in chains and specifying certificate types. HITs are represented as IPv6 addresses in the certificate extensions.
tldr.outcome: HIP implementations can exchange and verify certificates, enabling authentication and trust establishment, though this experimental approach was later refined in RFC 8002.

today: RFC 6253 is an Experimental RFC that was obsoleted by RFC 8002, which provides an updated specification for HIP certificates.

sections.title: Why Certificates Matter in HIP
sections.content: The Host Identity Protocol uses public-key cryptography to create a new namespace where each host's identity is derived directly from its public key. Unlike traditional Internet protocols that identify hosts by IP address, HIP hosts generate cryptographically verifiable statements using their private keys. To make this work, hosts need to exchange digital certificates that bind their identity information to their public keys. This document specifies how to transport those certificates inside HIP control packets, filling the placeholder that the original HIP specification left undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP uses special ID numbers based on math instead of network addresses. Computers need to exchange cards that prove those ID numbers are real, just like you might need to show an ID card to prove who you are.

sections.title: The CERT Parameter Structure
sections.content: The CERT parameter is a container with a fixed structure. It has a Type field (768), a Length field counting octets, and four key fields: Cert group (linking related certificates), Cert count (how many certificates are in the group), Cert ID (the sequence number within the group), and Cert Type (what kind of certificate this is). The parameter can appear multiple times in a HIP packet, and related certificates (such as a chain of certificates from a host up to a trusted root) are grouped together. Grouped certificates must be placed in order within HIP packets, and if a group spans multiple packets, the group must be marked as incomplete to prevent ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate container has labels like "this is certificate 2 out of 5" and "here is the type of ID card", so the receiver can put them in the right order and know they belong together.

sections.title: Certificate Types and Formats
sections.content: The RFC defines eight certificate types. Types 1 and 2 carry full certificates: X.509 v3 format (the standard Internet certificate format) and SPKI format (Simple Public Key Infrastructure, a certificate format used in some systems). Types 3 and 4 carry a cryptographic hash of the certificate and a URL, allowing receivers to fetch the certificate if needed. Types 5 and 6 carry LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) URLs pointing to the certificate. Types 7 and 8 carry only the certificate's Distinguished Name as a string, again allowing the receiver to retrieve the certificate from a directory. Using hash, URL, or name encodings results in smaller HIP packets but requires the receiver to resolve or cache the certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to send a certificate: the whole thing, a fingerprint with a web address, a directory address, or just a name. You pick the way that saves the most space but still lets the other computer find the real certificate.

sections.title: Representing Host Identities in Certificates
sections.content: Host Identity Tags (HITs) are represented as IPv6 addresses within X.509 v3 and SPKI certificates. In X.509 v3 certificates, when a HIP host signs a certificate with its private key, the HIT of the signer goes into the Issuer Alternative Name extension as an IPv6 address. When a certificate is issued for a HIP host identified by a HIT and Host Identifier (HI), the host's HIT goes into the Subject Alternative Name extension, and the full public key info is placed in the certificate's subject public key field. SPKI certificates represent HITs as S-expressions in the certificate, using the format (hash hit 2001:14:6cf:fae7:bb79:bf78:7d64:c056). This allows HIP hosts to authenticate each other by verifying that the certificate was signed by the claimed HIT and that the certificate was issued to the expected HIT.
sections.plainLanguage: To say "this certificate is from Alice" or "this certificate is for Bob" in an X.509 card, you write their HIP ID number (which looks like an IPv6 address). SPKI cards write it in a different format, but it means the same thing.

sections.title: Errors and When Certificates Matter
sections.content: If a HIP responder expects a certificate from the initiator but does not receive one, it may reject the connection and signal this by sending a HIP NOTIFY message with the CREDENTIALS_REQUIRED error type (value 48). If verification of a certificate fails (for example, the signature is invalid or the certificate is revoked), a HIP endpoint may send INVALID_CERTIFICATE (value 50). The NOTIFY message can optionally include identification of which certificate parameter failed, specified by its Cert group and Cert ID. However, the RFC does not define when or how certificates should be used in HIP authentication; that is left to other documents that build on this parameter specification. This means different HIP applications and extensions can define their own certificate policies.
sections.plainLanguage: If a computer needs a certificate from its partner and does not get one, it can send a message saying "give me your ID card." If the card looks fake or broken, it can send a message saying "that ID card is no good."

fields.desc: Length in octets, excluding Type, Length, and Padding.

fields.name: Cert Count
fields.desc: Total count of certificates in this group.

fields.name: Cert ID
fields.desc: Sequence number of this certificate in the group.
